title: Path MTU Discovery
subtitle: How a sender finds the biggest packet that fits the whole route, without anyone cutting it up.
summary: Path MTU Discovery lets a host find the largest IP datagram that can cross an entire route without being fragmented. The sender sets the Don't Fragment bit on everything it sends. A router that cannot forward a datagram that big drops it and returns an ICMP "fragmentation needed" message. RFC 1191 makes that message carry the size of the too-small link, in a new Next-Hop MTU field, so the sender can resize its packets right away.

eli5.summary: When you mail a big box through many post offices, you do not know which one has the smallest door. So you try anyway, and if a door is too small, the clerk sends back a note that says how wide it is. Then you pack a box that fits.

tldr.problem: Without a way to learn the smallest link size on a route, hosts either send tiny 576-byte datagrams everywhere or send larger ones that get fragmented.
tldr.mechanism: The sender sets the Don't Fragment bit and starts at its first-hop MTU. A router that cannot forward a datagram drops it and sends ICMP Type 3, Code 4, now carrying the Next-Hop MTU, and the sender shrinks its packets to match.
tldr.outcome: Hosts use the largest datagram the route allows and avoid fragmentation. The same idea carried over into IPv6 (RFC 8201).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When one host has a lot of data for another, it sends it as a series of IP datagrams. The RFC says it is "usually preferable" that these be as large as possible without needing fragmentation anywhere on the way. That size is the Path MTU (PMTU), and it equals the minimum of the MTUs of each hop in the path.

The RFC points out that the Internet protocol suite lacked "a standard mechanism for a host to discover the PMTU of an arbitrary path." A PMTU belongs to a path, which is a particular combination of source address, destination address and perhaps Type-of-Service. It is what the Host Requirements document (RFC 1122) calls the "Effective MTU for sending."

The RFC was written by Jeffrey Mogul and Steve Deering as the product of the IETF MTU Discovery Working Group, and it credits Geof Cooper with first suggesting the basic mechanism. It obsoletes RFC 1063, an earlier IP option-based approach.
sections.eli5: Imagine a road with several tunnels, and you are driving a truck. The roof of the lowest tunnel decides how tall your load can be for the whole trip. That lowest tunnel is the Path MTU.

sections.title: The Problem with Guessing
sections.content:
Before this RFC, the "current practice" was to use the lesser of 576 and the first-hop MTU for any destination that was not on the same network or subnet. That wastes capacity: many paths can carry far more than 576 octets, and a host sending much smaller datagrams than needed gets "suboptimal throughput."

It also fails in the other direction. Because some paths have a PMTU below 576, the old rule "does not prevent fragmentation in all cases."

Fragmentation is costly beyond the extra headers. The RFC cites the argument that it is harmful ("Fragmentation Considered Harmful" by Kent and Mogul), and notes a side benefit of PMTU Discovery: a host that does it will essentially never receive fragments from its peer, which helps with hosts that cannot reassemble them.

The authors expected routing protocols to eventually supply PMTU information within a routing area, but it was unclear when. So the Internet needed a mechanism that worked "before all hosts and routers are modified."
sections.eli5: Before, everybody just used a small safe box size, like always sending a tiny parcel even when a big one would fit. That is slow. Or they sent a big one and the post office chopped it into pieces, which is messy.

sections.title: How Discovery Works
sections.content:
The technique uses the Don't Fragment (DF) bit in the IP header. A source host first assumes the PMTU of a path is the known MTU of its first hop, and sends every datagram on that path with DF set.

If a router cannot forward a datagram without fragmenting it, it discards it and returns an ICMP Destination Unreachable message with the code "fragmentation needed and DF set." The RFC calls this a Datagram Too Big message. The source then lowers its assumed PMTU.

The existing message did not say how big the offending hop was. So the only change required of routers is that an unused header field now reports the MTU of the constricting hop.

Discovery ends when the host's estimate is low enough for delivery without fragmentation. The host may also stop discovery by ceasing to set DF. Normally it keeps setting DF so that, if the route changes and the new PMTU is lower, it will notice.

Start high
Begin with the first-hop MTU and set DF.
Learn from drops
Each Datagram Too Big message lowers the estimate.
Probe upward rarely
Periodically try larger sizes, since routes can improve.
sections.eli5: You start by trying your biggest box. Any post office that cannot handle it throws it back with a note saying "our door is this wide." You repack and try again. Now it goes through.

sections.title: The Router Change and Message Format
sections.content:
The router rule is short. When a router cannot forward a datagram because it exceeds the next-hop MTU and DF is set, it must return an ICMP Destination Unreachable message with Code 4. To support this technique, the router MUST put the next-hop MTU in the low-order 16 bits of the ICMP header field that was labelled "unused"; the high-order 16 bits stay zero.

The Next-Hop MTU is the size in octets of the largest datagram that could be forwarded, along the path of the original datagram, without being fragmented at this router. It includes the IP header and data but not lower-level headers. It never contains a value below 68, since every router must be able to forward a 68-octet datagram.

The rest of the message follows the usual ICMP pattern: the Internet header of the original datagram plus the first 64 bits of its data, so the sender can tell which datagram was dropped.
sections.eli5: The note that comes back has a few boxes to fill in: what kind of note it is, why, and one new box that says how wide the small door is. A router that does not fill in the new box leaves it as zero.

sections.title: What Hosts Must Do
sections.content:
On receiving a Datagram Too Big message, a host MUST reduce its PMTU estimate using the Next-Hop MTU, and MUST avoid eliciting more such messages soon. It may shrink its datagrams or stop setting DF. The RFC deliberately does not prescribe the exact behavior.

Three firm limits apply. A host MUST never reduce its estimate below 68 octets. It MUST NOT raise its estimate because of what a Datagram Too Big message says. And it must cope with messages from unmodified routers, recognizable by a zero Next-Hop MTU.

To notice increases, a host may try a larger size again, but "at infrequent intervals." It must not try less than 5 minutes after a Datagram Too Big message, or less than 1 minute after a previous successful increase. The RFC recommends twice those values: 10 minutes and 2 minutes.

TCP. A host doing PMTU Discovery must not send datagrams larger than 576 octets unless the receiver allows it. For TCP, that means no more than 40 octets plus the peer's MSS. Hosts SHOULD stop lowering the MSS they advertise to 536 for non-local peers, since doing so prevents discovery of PMTUs above 576.
sections.eli5: The sender has rules. Always listen to the note and pack smaller. Never go below the tiniest allowed box. And do not believe a note that says you may use a bigger box. Now and then, quietly try a bigger one anyway, but not too often.

sections.title: Old Routers and Implementation Advice
sections.content:
Sections 5 to 7 of the RFC are advice, not requirements. For old-style messages with a zero Next-Hop MTU, the simplest strategy is to fall back to 576 and stop setting DF. A binary search converges but is complex to implement, and multiplying by a constant like 0.75 is explicitly not recommended.

The recommended strategy uses a table of "plateaus," a short list of common MTUs. The host picks the greatest plateau less than the Total Length returned in the ICMP message. The plateaus run from 65535 down through 32000, 17914, 8166, 4352, 2002, 1492, 1006, 508 and 296 to 68. With it, going from an FDDI MTU to an Ethernet MTU takes only two round-trip times.

For where to keep the result, the RFC suggests the IP layer store PMTU values in per-host routing entries, with ICMP processing the messages and transport layers being notified of decreases. Stale entries should be aged: after about 10 minutes without a decrease, the estimate is reset to the first-hop MTU. The RFC also notes that routers derived from 4.2BSD report an inflated Total Length.

The plateau table is "an implementation suggestion, NOT a specification or requirement," and the RFC expects its higher values to go out of date.
sections.eli5: Some old post offices forget to write down the door width. Then you guess by trying a short list of common sizes, from big to small, until a box gets through. You also forget what you learned after about ten minutes, in case the route got better.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism opens two denial-of-service attacks, both based on forged Datagram Too Big messages sent to a host.

In the first, a forged message claims a PMTU far below reality. Data would still flow, because the victim never sets its estimate below the absolute minimum, but at only 8 octets of IP data per datagram, progress could be slow.

In the second, a forged message claims a PMTU above reality. If believed, it would cause datagrams to be dropped by some router until the host rediscovered the mistake within one round-trip time. The defense is the rule from the host section: a host should never raise its estimate based on a Datagram Too Big message, so it is not vulnerable to this variant.

The RFC adds that an attacker who could block legitimate Datagram Too Big messages from arriving would have simpler denial-of-service attacks available anyway.
sections.eli5: A prankster could send you a fake note saying the door is tiny, so you send only crumbs. Or a fake note saying the door is huge. The rules make you ignore the second kind, and the first kind can only slow you down so far.

today: Path MTU Discovery is a standard part of IP stacks. Its IPv6 counterpart is specified in RFC 8201 (which obsoletes RFC 1981), and RFC 4821 describes a variant that does not depend on ICMP messages being delivered. Operators commonly see it as ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages, and filtering those messages is a well-known cause of connections that hang on large packets.
